v1363: Ephesians 4:2-3|Forbearing one another in love; endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
v1365: Draw your fight cycle together on paper.
v1366: The psalmist prayed, "Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts" (Psalm 139:23). This is not a request for a harsh inspection. It is the prayer of a child who trusts a Father who already knows everything and still loves completely. Lamentations 3:40 invites us to search and try our ways, and Proverbs 20:5 says a person of understanding draws out the deep purposes of the heart. Keeping a seven-day body log is a practical way of praying this prayer. Because there is no condemnation for those in Christ, you can look honestly at your tension, your sleep and your unfinished worries without fear. Telling someone safe what you found also brings you into the body of Christ, where burdens are meant to be shared rather than hidden.
v1367: Research suggests that a body which stays tense is usually responding to something, even when you cannot name it. The stress system, sometimes called the HPA axis, releases cortisol and adrenaline when the brain senses threat. If the threat is hidden and ongoing, such as a difficult relationship, constant news, late screens, too much caffeine, poor sleep or a physical problem, the alarm never fully switches off. Rating your tension three times a day and writing what happened in the hour before moves this hidden pattern into awareness. That engages the prefrontal cortex, the planning part of the brain, which helps calm the alarm. Circling the highest moments after a week turns vague dread into a clear target. Over the following weeks, working on one cause at a time teaches your nervous system that its signals are heard and acted on.
v1368: God made your body to speak. Tension in the jaw, a tight chest or a churning stomach are not enemies but messengers, built by a Creator who wants you to notice when something is wrong. He did not design you to live in a fog, carrying unnamed weight. Haggai 1:5 says, "Consider your ways," and God invites that reflection because He wants to lead you into wholeness, not shame. He also designed us to discover ourselves in relationship. When you share your log with a trusted friend, a spouse or a counsellor, you reflect the God who is Father, Son and Spirit, always in loving communion. Self-knowledge received with grace becomes the first step toward rest, and the God who searches you is the same God who heals what He finds.
v1369: When Elijah collapsed in exhaustion and fear, God did not lecture him. "An angel touched him, and said unto him, Arise and eat" (1 Kings 19:5). God gave him sleep, food, gentle touch and time before He spoke about the next task. Ecclesiastes 3:4 reminds us there is a time to weep and a time to laugh, and Psalm 30:5 promises that joy comes in the morning. Jesus says, "Come unto me, all ye that labour" (Matthew 11:28). Completing the stress cycle follows this pattern of care. You move, you receive comfort, you notice your body settle, and you thank God that you are safe right now. The problem may still be there, but your Father meets your body first, just as He met Elijah under the tree.
v1370: Research suggests that stress hormones like adrenaline and cortisol prepare the body to run or fight. When we sit at a desk or lie awake worrying, those chemicals keep circulating and the body stays braced. Brisk movement, such as walking fast, dancing, cycling or climbing stairs, uses up that energy and tells the body it has done what it was preparing to do. Then a calming signal finishes the job. A twenty-second hug, a good cry, real laughter or slow breathing activates the calming branch of the nervous system, which slows the heart and lets digestion and repair return. Noticing your shoulders drop helps the brain record that safety. Done on stressful days for several weeks, this trains your system to return to rest more quickly instead of staying stuck in alarm.
v1371: God designed us as whole people, not minds floating above bodies. He built rhythms of effort and rest into creation, day and night, work and Sabbath, and He made our bodies to rise to a challenge and then come back down. A stress response that never ends was never His plan. He also made comfort deeply relational. A hug from someone who loves us, tears that are received, and laughter shared with friends are gifts that carry His tenderness to our nervous systems. Thanking God at the end of the cycle connects the felt safety in your body with the true safety of being His child. This is how He heals, not only by solving problems from a distance but by drawing near, touching, feeding and restoring His weary children.
v1372: Scripture honours the body. Paul writes, "Your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost" (1 Corinthians 6:19). Caring for it is an act of worship, not a lack of faith. Luke, who wrote one of the Gospels, is called "the beloved physician" in Colossians 4:14, which shows that God has always worked through medical skill. John prayed that his friend would "be in health, even as thy soul prospereth" (3 John 1:2), and Proverbs 17:22 links a merry heart with healing. Getting a health check is not choosing doctors over God. It is receiving the care God provides through people and knowledge. Seeing a doctor, following treatment and continuing calming practices together reflect a faith that trusts God with both the spiritual and the physical sides of life.
v1373: Research suggests that many physical conditions produce feelings that look exactly like anxiety or chronic stress. An overactive thyroid speeds up the heart and makes you shaky. Anaemia or low iron leaves you exhausted and breathless. Low vitamin B12 or D can affect mood and energy. Blood sugar swings trigger adrenaline, which causes sweating and panic. Sleep apnoea interrupts breathing through the night, so the stress system fires again and again while you sleep. Caffeine, energy drinks, nicotine and some medicines can also push the body into alert. Listing your symptoms and how long they have lasted helps a doctor find the cause. When a physical problem is treated, the whole nervous system often settles, and your calming practices begin to work far better over the following weeks.
v1374: God made us as integrated beings, where body, mind and spirit affect one another. This is why a thyroid problem can feel like fear, and why prayer and peace can ease physical tension. He did not design us to blame ourselves for symptoms that have a bodily cause. Some believers carry shame, thinking their racing heart proves weak faith, when the truth is their body needs care. God's character is kind and practical. He fed hungry crowds, healed real bodies and cared about physical needs, not only spiritual ones. Getting checked is a way of agreeing with His design. Wholeness, in the biblical sense of shalom, includes healthy blood, rested lungs and a steady heart. Your Father wants you well, and He invites you to use every good gift He has given.
v1375: Peter writes, "Casting all your care upon him, for he careth for you" (1 Peter 5:7). The reason we can hand over our worries is relational. God is not a distant manager but a caring Father. Psalm 55:22 says, "Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee." Jesus offers to share the yoke with us so that the load becomes light (Matthew 11:28-30), and Philippians 4:6-7 promises peace that guards our hearts when we pray with thanksgiving. Sorting your worries into "Mine to do" and "Not mine to control" puts this trust into practice. You take responsibility for small next steps, which honours your calling, and you release the rest into the hands of One who never sleeps and never drops what He is given.
v1376: Research suggests that an unresolved list of threats keeps the brain's alarm system scanning. The amygdala, which watches for danger, does not easily tell the difference between a real threat and an unfinished worry, so it keeps the stress hormones flowing. Writing every worry on paper moves it out of short-term memory, which lowers mental load. Naming one small next step with a time gives the planning part of the brain a clear task, and that sense of control calms the alarm. Praying over the things you cannot control reduces the feeling of carrying danger alone, which is one of the strongest reasons bodies stay in stress mode. Practised regularly for several weeks, this habit helps your nervous system learn that it can set things down and still be safe.
v1377: God never designed us to carry the whole world on our shoulders. Only He is all-powerful and all-knowing, and when we try to hold everything, our bodies show the strain. His design is that we live as children who depend on a good Father, doing our part faithfully and trusting Him with the rest. This is freeing, not lazy. It mirrors the way Jesus lived, working hard yet withdrawing to pray and placing even His suffering into the Father's hands. Handing over the load also restores relationship. Worry often isolates us, but prayer brings us back into conversation with God. Closing the page and resting is a small act of faith that says, "You are God, and I am not." In that surrender, our bodies and hearts find room to breathe.
v1378: "For so he giveth his beloved sleep" (Psalm 127:2). Sleep is a gift from a Father to His beloved children, not a reward for finishing everything. From the start, creation followed a rhythm: "the evening and the morning were the first day" (Genesis 1:5). Psalm 4:8 says, "I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety." When Jesus saw His disciples worn out, He told them to come apart and rest a while (Mark 6:31). An evening downshift lives out this truth. Choosing a stop time, writing tomorrow's worries down and praying over them, and going to bed at a similar hour each night are ways of receiving God's gift of rest instead of fighting it.
v1379: Research suggests that the body has an internal clock which raises cortisol in the morning to wake us and lowers it at night so we can sleep. Bright screens, late work and worry confuse this clock and keep alertness high when the body should be winding down. Dimming lights and stopping screens thirty to sixty minutes before bed helps the brain release melatonin, the sleep hormone. A warm shower, stretching or quiet music signal safety to the nervous system. Writing worries on paper stops the mind from rehearsing them in bed. Slow breathing with long out-breaths activates the calming branch of the nervous system. Over several weeks, a consistent bedtime trains the body clock, so falling asleep becomes easier and deep, restoring sleep becomes more frequent.
v1380: God designed us to live in rhythms because He is a God of order and care. The sun sets each evening as a daily reminder that we are not meant to work without end. Sleep itself is an act of trust, since we become completely helpless and must leave the world in God's hands while we rest. By building a calm transition each evening, we agree with His design and admit our limits. This is good for relationships too, because a rested person is more patient, kind and present with family. God, who neither slumbers nor sleeps, keeps watch over us so that we can lie down. Each evening downshift becomes a quiet confession that He is faithful, and that we are His beloved, safe to rest.
v1381: "The LORD is my shepherd, I shall not want. He maketh me to lie down in green pastures" (Psalm 23:1-2). David's picture of God is deeply relational. A shepherd walks with the sheep, leads them to safety and stays close in dark valleys. Psalm 91:1-2 calls God our refuge and fortress, and Isaiah 26:3 promises perfect peace to the one whose mind is stayed on Him. Psalm 4:8 says it is the LORD who makes us dwell in safety. For people who have lived through danger, knowing these truths in the head is not always enough. This practice invites the truth to reach the body. Reading Psalm 23 slowly and saying, "The Lord is my shepherd. Right now, I am safe," lets your adoption as God's child become something you can feel.
v1382: Research suggests that the nervous system decides whether we are safe mostly through felt signals, not facts. Someone who has lived through trauma or long stress may know they are safe but still feel on guard, because the body learned to expect danger. Slow out-breaths calm the heart through the vagus nerve. Picturing peaceful images like green pastures and still waters gives the brain a sense of safety it can feel. Noticing one place in your body that feels even a little calm and staying with it strengthens the brain's safety pathway. Over weeks, this widens the window of tolerance, the zone in which you can handle stress without becoming overwhelmed or shut down. Small, repeated experiences of felt safety slowly retrain a body that has forgotten how to rest.
v1383: God made us to know Him not only with our minds but with our whole being, including our bodies. He chose to reveal Himself through pictures we can feel, a shepherd, a refuge, a mother hen gathering chicks, because He knows that we heal through experience and relationship. A wounded body learns safety the same way a frightened child does, through a steady, gentle presence over time. God is that presence. He is patient with nervous systems that still flinch, and He never shames us for needing to feel safe. Resting in silence before Him is like a child resting in a parent's arms. Each time you do this, you let His love go deeper than thought, into the places where fear once lived, and you move toward the wholeness He intends.
